warnings: Lesson is long at 4820 words; consider tightening for reading flow.

improvement_notes: Reduce repetition around optional readiness services and the distinction between action goal acceptance and final results. The point is important, but it is restated many times across the Actions, Worked Robotics Example, Python Lab, Mini Simulation, Common Mistakes, quiz answers, and vocabulary.

Shorten the lesson or divide it into a core lesson plus an advanced engineering notes section. The current volume is unusually high for a mental-model introduction and may overload beginners before they have used ROS 2 directly.

Add a compact comparison table for node, topic, service, and action near the beginning. The distinctions are currently accurate but distributed across many sections, increasing working-memory demands.

Make the action lifecycle in the Python lab more complete if the lesson intends to teach actions rather than only goal acceptance. A minimal simulated feedback callback, cancellation path, and final result would align the code more fully with the conceptual model; alternatively, label the class explicitly as a goal-acceptance-only abstraction in the learning objectives.

Clarify that topic commands such as velocity commands are often subject to command timeout or watchdog behavior and are not automatically safe merely because they use a topic. The later safety caveat is good but could be connected directly to the cmd_velocity example earlier.

Add one worked learner exercise that changes QoS-like assumptions, message age, or queue behavior. The lesson mentions QoS and executor effects accurately, but students do not experimentally observe any of them in the provided simulation.

The generated visuals are relevant and well captioned, but the workshop illustration may reinforce analogy more than technical structure. Prioritize the schematic and communication graph, and ensure the visual labels remain legible at lesson-reading size.

Consider adding a glossary note distinguishing a ROS 2 node from a generic software component. The current wording is defensible and beginner-friendly, but the repeated phrase 'logical runtime entity' could be paired once with the formal ROS 2 interpretation.

linkedin.title: ROS 2 Mental Model: Nodes, Topics, Services, and Actions
linkedin.description: A practical robotics lesson that connects behavior trees to ROS 2 communication, with a Python simulation for topics, services, actions, stale data, and timeouts.
linkedin.commentary:
A behavior tree can decide that a robot should dock—but it does not need to contain the camera driver, battery monitor, motor controller, or docking implementation.

This lesson introduces the ROS 2 communication model through RoboRover:

• Nodes organize focused software responsibilities.
• Topics carry recurring observations and commands.
• Services handle short, bounded request-and-response operations.
• Actions manage longer tasks with acceptance, feedback, cancellation, and a final result.

The accompanying Python simulation makes the concepts testable without requiring a ROS 2 installation. Students observe fresh versus stale battery data, service unavailability, action-goal acceptance, and the importance of timeouts and failure behavior.

Try the graph-design activity, predict the program’s decisions, then extend the lab with an emergency-state branch or a dashboard subscriber. The goal is not to memorize interface names, but to choose communication patterns that match the timing and failure needs of a real robot.
